newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson exits from Great Western takeover battle.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson exits from Great Western takeover battle.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson and Co. dropped its $6.9 billion hostile bid for Great Western Financial Corp. Wednesday, ending a bitter savings-and-loan takeover battle and clearing the way for Great Western to merge with friendly suitor Washington Mutual Inc.
The move was a blow to Ahmanson, which had waged a bitter campaign to acquire the rival California thrift in an effort to remain independent in the rapidly consoliating market.
By walking away empty-handed, Ahmanson itself now becomes vulnerable to a takeover by an out-of-state bank or even the Great Western/Washington Mutual combined entity.

"The countdown has started to see how much longer Ahmanson can remain independent," said analyst Charlotte Chamberlain of Jefferies and Co. "My sense is there's just one trophy thrift franchise left in California with market share above 5 percent and it's Home Savings."
Ahmanson owns Home Savings.
Some experts said a logical next step may be for Washington Mutual to acquire Ahmanson once it absorbs Great Western.
"There's clearly speculation a combined Wamu/Great Western could take a run at Ahmanson. Some of the same synergies presumably apply," said Leslie Nelkin of Furman Selz.

Irwindale, Calif.-based Ahmanson threw in the towel after the Delaware Chancery court Tuesday denied its motion to delay a June 13 shareholder vote on Great Western's proposed $6.87 billion transaction with Washington Mutual.

Ahmanson had hoped to buy time to rally more support for its bid, but the ruling left few options for Ahmanson, which had already raised its bid once and would dilute shareholder value if it raised it again.
In a statement issued early Wednesday, Ahmanson Chairman Charles Rinehart said the company concluded it could not win without raising its bid.
"We still believe that Great Western was an attractive partner, but not at the expense of returns to shareholders," Rinehart said.

A spokeswoman for Ahmanson said it would take a second-quarter charge for costs associated with the bid. In the year-ago second quarter, Ahmanson reported net income of $68.7 million, or 50 cents a share on a fully diluted basis.

Ahmanson initially launched its offer in February. Great Western, based in Chatsworth, Calif., rejected the bid and on March 6 announced it agreed to be bought by Washington Mutual in a deal that would create the largest U.S. thrift, with $86 billion in assets.

Washington Mutual and Great Western said Wednesday they were pleased Ahmanson had withdrawn and they expect to close the merger within weeks of stockholder and regulatory approval, which is expected by late June or early July.
Ahmanson's stock jumped $1.25 to $41.50 on the New York Stock Exchange. Great Western rose $1.375 to $48.75 on the NYSE while Washington Mutual added $1.0625 to $54.8125 on Nasdaq.
Tuesday's Delaware court ruling was the last straw for Ahmanson in its 3-1/2-month pursuit of Great Western, which played out in court and in numerous meetings with investors, analysts and the press.

"They were basically a frustrated, hostile bidder whose bid was not worth significantly more (than Washington Mutual's)," said Steven Cohen, partner with Kellner, DiLeo and Co, a New York-based merger and arbitrage firm.
The battle took on a surprisingly personal tone with Great Western accusing Ahmanson of planning to lay off thousands of Great Western employees in order to make the merger work.
While Ahmanson's bid held a premium to Washington Mutual's for a while, Washington Mutual succeeded in persuading investors its deal was superior.

Both bids fluctuated, based on the value of the stocks. Ahmanson raised its bid and was offering up to 1.2 of its shares for each Great Western share, while Washington Mutual's deal called for an exchange of 0.9 of a share for each Great Western share.
Based on Wednesday's prices, Ahmanson's bid was actually valued higher at $49.80 a share, while Washington Mutual's bid was worth $49.33 a share.

However, analysts said investors favoured Seattle-based Washington Mutual's bid because it is a friendly transaction endorsed by Great Western's board and because of Washington Mutual Chairman Kerry Killinger's reputation and success in executing acquisitions, a total of 22 in the last 10 years.
Indeed, Ahmanson never even made it to the negotiating table, and Rinehart spoke only once with Great Western Chief Executive John Maher during the entire dogfight.
That conversation occurred on the night of Feb. 17, when he called Maher to tell him he would be making the initial bid the following day.
Ahmanson argued that because both it and Great Western were located in the same geographic area, it could wring more expense reductions from a combination.
But Washington Mutual cited its record of successful acquisitions and said it could cut expenses and grow revenue at the same time.
Rinehart said Ahmanson will pursue its strategy to grow as a full-service bank for consumers and small business.
